linux.html.title: DMI / SMBIOS, FRU & Motherboard Inventory
linux.html.subtitle: dmidecode SMBIOS tables, chassis serial/SKU, BIOS revision, DIMM slot mapping & PSU FRUs

commands.desc: Query system manufacturer, product name, service tag / serial number, UUID & BIOS revision
commands.details: Reads the motherboard SMBIOS/DMI table directly via /dev/mem or /sys/firmware/dmi/tables. Essential for verifying server asset tags, chassis serial numbers, motherboard revision, and BIOS firmware version without rebooting or logging into the BMC.
commands.tip: Instant FRU / Serial lookup
flags: DMI Type 1: System Manufacturer, Product Name, Serial Number, SKU & UUID
DMI Type 0: BIOS Vendor, Version, Release Date & firmware revision
DMI Type 2: Motherboard model, serial, asset tag & physical location
DMI Type 3: Rack chassis type, lock status, serial & height (U)
subs: Print only the server chassis/system serial number
Print only the server model (e.g. PowerEdge, ProLiant, Supermicro)
Print only the active BIOS version and release date
DMI Type 9: List all physical PCIe riser slots and whether each slot is In Use or Available
commands.rootWhy: reads the firmware DMI tables (/sys/firmware/dmi/tables/DMI is 0400 root)
copy:
# needs root
dmidecode -t system -t bios -t baseboard -t chassis

commands.cmd: dmidecode -t memory | grep -E 'Size:|Locator:|Bank Locator:|Type:|Speed:|Configured Memory Speed:|Manufacturer:|Serial Number:|Part Number:'
commands.desc: Inspect physical RAM DIMM slots, populated vs empty sockets, DDR speed, manufacturer & part numbers
commands.details: Queries DMI Type 16 (Physical Memory Array) and Type 17 (Memory Device). Crucial for data center techs replacing a faulty DIMM or verifying that all populated channels are running at their rated MT/s speed and matching part numbers.
commands.tip: Maps OS to motherboard silkscreen
flags: DMI Types 16 & 17: Physical memory array capacity and individual DIMM slot details
Silkscreened motherboard DIMM slot label (e.g., PROC 1 DIMM 1A, P0_MC0_DIMM_A0)
Actual negotiated DDR4/DDR5 transfer rate (check for downclocking)
subs: Show maximum supported memory capacity, error correction type (Multi-bit ECC), and total slot count
Compact list of every motherboard DIMM slot and whether it is populated or 'No Module Installed'
Concise summary of system RAM banks and populated DIMM sizes
commands.rootWhy: reads the firmware DMI tables (/sys/firmware/dmi/tables/DMI is 0400 root)
copy:
# needs root
dmidecode -t memory | grep -E 'Size:|Locator:|Bank Locator:|Type:|Speed:|Configured Memory Speed:|Manufacturer:|Serial Number:|Part Number:'

commands.desc: Inspect redundant Power Supply Units (PSU wattage, serial, status) and CPU socket population
commands.details: DMI Type 39 reports installed server power supplies, their max power capacity (e.g., 1600W/2400W), part/serial numbers, and whether each PSU is Present and OK. DMI Type 4 reports physical CPU sockets, voltage, external clock, and enabled core counts.
flags: DMI Type 39: System Power Supply (Status, Plugged/Unplugged, Max Power Capacity)
DMI Type 4: Socket designation (CPU0/CPU1), family, voltage, max/current speed
subs: Print exact CPU model strings for all populated sockets
Read product name and serial without root if permissions allow (/sys/class/dmi/id/)
commands.rootWhy: reads the firmware DMI tables (/sys/firmware/dmi/tables/DMI is 0400 root)

commands.desc: Generate complete hardware inventory tree with bus addresses (PCI/USB/SCSI/NVMe) and driver status
commands.details: Probes DMI, sysfs, PCI, USB, and storage subsystems to map physical hardware paths (e.g., pci@0000:3b:00.0) to Linux device names (eth0, nvme0n1) and hardware classes. Spots 'UNCLAIMED' devices missing a kernel driver.
commands.tip: Look for UNCLAIMED devices
flags: Include PCI/USB/SCSI/NVMe bus addresses for physical slot tracing
subs: List all NIC ports with PCIe bus address, logical interface name, MAC, and link state
List all storage controllers (RAID/HBA/NVMe) and attached physical disks
Export full machine-readable hardware manifest for DCIM asset ingestion
commands.rootWhy: runs as a user but leaves most hardware out: run as root for the full picture

linux.html.title: PCIe Bus, Link Speed/Width, CPU & NUMA Topology
linux.html.subtitle: lspci link training verification (Gen3/4/5 GT/s & x16/x8), AER errors, CPU & NUMA affinity

commands.desc: Verify PCIe negotiated link speed (GT/s) and lane width (x16/x8) vs device capability (LnkCap vs LnkSta)
commands.details: Compares what a PCIe card (GPU, NIC, NVMe HBA) is capable of (LnkCap: Speed 16GT/s or 32GT/s, Width x16) against what it actually negotiated with the motherboard riser (LnkSta). If LnkSta shows 'Downgraded', reseat the card/riser or inspect gold fingers for debris.
commands.tip: Detects bad risers / unseated cards
flags: Maximum verbosity (required to decode PCIe configuration space registers)
Hardware maximum rated PCIe link speed (8GT/s=Gen3, 16GT/s=Gen4, 32GT/s=Gen5) and width
Currently trained PCIe speed & width (flags '(downgraded)' if lanes failed training)
subs: Scan all PCIe devices across the server for any downgraded PCIe lane width or speed
List all PCIe devices with Vendor:Device hex IDs [10de:2330] and active kernel driver
Render PCIe root complex, bridges, switches, and endpoints as a tree
commands.rootWhy: capabilities (LnkSta, AER, DevCtl) show <access denied> unless root

commands.desc: Inspect PCIe Advanced Error Reporting (AER) counters and hot-rescan the PCIe bus
commands.details: UESta (Uncorrectable Error Status) and CESta (Correctable Error Status) show PCIe link-level CRC errors, receiver errors, bad TLP/DLLP, or surprise link down events. Writing '1' to /sys/bus/pci/rescan re-enumerates the PCIe bus if a card or U.2 NVMe drive dropped offline.
flags: Uncorrectable PCIe errors (DLP, SDES, TLP, FCP, CmpltTO, UnxCmplt, MalfTLP)
Correctable PCIe errors (RxErr, BadTLP, BadDLLP, Rollover, Timeout)
Trigger kernel PCIe bus rescan without rebooting
subs: Safely hot-remove a specific PCIe BDF device before hot-swapping or rescanning
Read raw PCI configuration space COMMAND register in hex
commands.rootWhy: capabilities (LnkSta, AER, DevCtl) show <access denied> unless root
copy:
# needs root
lspci -vvv | grep -E '^[0-9a-f]|UESta:|CESta:' && echo 1 | tee /sys/bus/pci/rescan

commands.desc: Inspect CPU socket topology, physical cores vs SMT threads, cache hierarchy, and CPU flags
commands.details: Displays complete processor architecture, sockets, NUMA nodes, L1/L2/L3 cache sizes, virtualization support (VT-x / AMD-V), and per-core frequency scaling limits. Use 'lscpu -e' to verify all cores are ONLINE and running at expected boost clocks.
flags: Extended human-readable table mapping every logical vCPU to NUMA node, Socket, and Core
Verify no CPU cores have been offlined due to hardware faults
Maximum turbo clock frequency reported by ACPI/cpufreq
subs: Inspect active CPU frequency governor (performance vs powersave) and hardware P-states
Lock all CPU cores to the 'performance' governor for low-latency datacenter workloads
Check loaded CPU microcode patch version and current clock speed

commands.desc: View NUMA node memory allocation, inter-socket latency matrix, and pin processes to a NUMA node
commands.details: On dual-socket or multi-chiplet EPYC/Xeon servers, accessing RAM or PCIe devices attached to a remote CPU socket traverses the UPI/Infinity Fabric interconnect, adding latency. 'numactl --hardware' shows free/total RAM per node and node distance costs.
commands.tip: Match NIC/GPU to local NUMA node
flags: Display available NUMA nodes, CPU list per node, node memory size, and distance matrix
Show per-node meminfo table (MemTotal, MemFree, HugePages) in MiB
subs: Pin a process strictly to CPU cores and local RAM on NUMA node 0
Check which CPU NUMA node a specific NIC or NVMe device is physically wired to
Render ASCII topology diagram of NUMA nodes, PCIe bridges, NICs, NVMe drives, and caches (hwloc-nox)

linux.html.title: ECC Memory, EDAC, MCE & Thermal Triage
linux.html.subtitle: edac-util DIMM fault isolation, rasdaemon MCE logs, ipmi/lm-sensors thermals & turbostat power

commands.desc: Check Error Detection and Correction (EDAC) memory controllers for Correctable (CE) & Uncorrectable (UE) ECC errors
commands.details: Reads the Linux kernel EDAC subsystem to pinpoint exactly which memory controller (mc0/mc1), channel, and DIMM label is logging single-bit Correctable Errors (CE) or multi-bit Uncorrectable Errors (UE). High CE rates indicate a degrading DIMM that should be scheduled for replacement.
commands.tip: Pinpoints bad DIMM slot in OS
flags: Verbose summary of all memory controllers, chip-select rows, and error counts
Motherboard silkscreen label mapped by EDAC driver
Cumulative single-bit (CE) and multi-bit (UE) ECC error counters since boot
subs: Check whether the kernel EDAC driver is loaded and monitoring memory controllers
Directly read per-DIMM labels and ECC error counts from sysfs (zero dependencies)

commands.desc: Query Ubuntu rasdaemon hardware error database for Memory ECC, PCIe AER, and CPU Machine Check Exceptions (MCE)
commands.details: On modern Ubuntu servers, 'rasdaemon' replaces legacy 'mcelog' to record all hardware Reliability, Availability, and Serviceability (RAS) trace events into a persistent SQLite database (/var/lib/rasdaemon/ras-mc_event.db), preserving errors across reboots.
flags: Aggregate count of Memory Controller, PCIe AER, Extlog, and CPU MCE errors
Print detailed timestamped log of every recorded hardware error event
subs: Display mainboard vendor and model recognized by rasdaemon DIMM label database
Inspect recent hardware error alerts logged by the rasdaemon systemd unit
Search kernel ring buffer for ACPI APEI/GHES firmware-first hardware errors
commands.rootWhy: reads the machine-check / rasdaemon records

commands.desc: Monitor CPU package/core temperatures, NVMe composite temps, VRM voltages & chassis sensors
commands.details: Uses lm-sensors (coretemp / k10temp / drivetemp) and kernel thermal zones (millidegrees Celsius) to check if a server is overheating due to a failed heatsink fan, dried thermal paste, or blocked rack airflow.
flags: Read all hwmon sensors (CPU Package id 0/1, core temps, NVMe composite temp)
subs: Live 1-second refresh of all CPU and board temperature sensors
Check if CPU0 has experienced core or package thermal throttling events since boot

commands.desc: Real-time x86 CPU telemetry: actual core MHz, busy%, C-state residency, SMI interrupts & package wattage
commands.details: Reads hardware Model-Specific Registers (MSRs) directly. Essential for diagnosing servers that feel 'slow': reveals if BIOS System Management Interrupts (SMI) are stalling cores, if CPU power capping is throttling frequency (Bzy_MHz), or how many Watts CPU & RAM are drawing.
commands.tip: From linux-tools-common package
flags: Print single aggregated system summary line per interval instead of 100+ core lines
Actual average clock speed (MHz) while cores are actively executing instructions
BIOS System Management Interrupt count (non-zero spikes indicate firmware/ECC stalls)
Real-time RAPL power consumption in Watts for CPU sockets and DRAM

linux.html.title: Enterprise NVMe, SMART, RAID & Drive Bay LEDs
linux.html.subtitle: nvme-cli health/wear/format, smartctl SAS/SATA triage, mdadm RAID rebuilds & ledctl drive locator

commands.desc: List all NVMe namespaces (model, serial, FW) and inspect SMART health log for wear, spare & media errors
commands.details: Queries NVMe admin controller logs. For datacenter drive replacement triage, check 'critical_warning' (must be 0), 'available_spare' vs 'available_spare_threshold', 'percentage_used' (endurance wear), 'media_errors' (unrecovered NAND reads), and 'unsafe_shutdowns'.
commands.tip: Check media_errors & percentage_used
flags: Tabular list of all /dev/nvmeXnY block devices, serial numbers, capacities, and firmware
Read NVMe SMART / Health Information Log (Log Page 02h)
Count of unrecovered data integrity errors on NAND media (non-zero = replace drive)
subs: Inspect recent controller command errors and status codes
Identify controller model (mn), serial (sn), firmware revision (fr), and total NVM capacity
Display NVMe multipath subsystems and PCIe BDF addresses for each controller
commands.rootWhy: opens the NVMe controller node (/dev/nvmeX is 0600 root)
copy:
# needs root
nvme list && nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0

commands.desc: Cryptographically secure-erase an enterprise NVMe drive or update controller firmware online
commands.details: Executes an NVMe Format NVM Admin command. '--ses=1' performs a User Data Erase; '--ses=2' performs an instant Cryptographic Erase by destroying and regenerating the internal media encryption key. Can also switch logical block size (4096B vs 512B) via '--lbaf'.
flags: Secure Erase Setting: 1 = User Data Erase, 2 = Cryptographic Erase (instant key wipe)
LBA Format index (check 'nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1' for 512B vs 4K sector formats)
subs: Check supported sector sizes (512B vs 4096B 4Kn) and active LBA format
Download firmware image to NVMe controller and activate it on slot 1
Discard (TRIM/Deallocate) all blocks on an SSD/NVMe device prior to re-partitioning
commands.rootWhy: opens the NVMe controller node (/dev/nvmeX is 0600 root)

commands.desc: Inspect SATA/SAS/NVMe SMART health attributes, grown defect lists, and trigger background self-tests
commands.details: Reads complete SMART and extended device statistics. On SATA drives, check IDs 5 (Reallocated_Sector_Ct), 187 (Reported_Uncorrect), 197 (Current_Pending_Sector), and 198 (Offline_Uncorrectable). On SAS drives, check 'Elements in grown defect list' and 'Non-medium error count'.
commands.tip: Watch Reallocated & Pending sectors
flags: Print all SMART + Extended info (error logs, self-test history, Phy event counters)
Print brief SMART overall-health self-assessment test result (PASSED / FAILED)
Print standard SMART attributes, capabilities, and error logs
subs: Run a 2-minute captive/background short self-test and view test log results
Query physical disk #0 behind a Broadcom/LSI MegaRAID hardware RAID controller
Scan and list all SMART-capable storage devices and RAID enclosures
commands.rootWhy: opens the drive and sends raw SMART / pass-through commands

commands.desc: Inspect Linux software RAID (mdadm) array health, sync progress, and hot-swap a failed disk
commands.details: Shows active mdraid personalities (RAID1/RAID5/RAID6/RAID10), member disk states ([UU] = healthy, [U_] = degraded), and rebuild speed. When replacing a failed drive in a rack server, mark it faulty, remove it, physically swap the sled, and re-add the replacement.
flags: Live kernel status of all active md RAID arrays and rebuild percentage
Detailed array UUID, layout, state (clean/degraded/recovering), and member disk roles
subs: Mark a failing partition as faulty and detach it from /dev/md0 before physical drive pull
Add newly inserted replacement drive partition into /dev/md0 to start rebuild
Inspect RAID superblocks directly on member partitions
Save active RAID array definitions to mdadm.conf and update Ubuntu initramfs
commands.rootWhy: works on block devices or device-mapper, which are root-only

commands.desc: Blink physical drive bay Fault/Locate LEDs (ledctl) and map SCSI/SAS HBA enclosure slots
commands.details: In a 24-bay server chassis, pulling the wrong drive can take down an array. 'ledctl' (from 'ledmon' package) drives SGPIO/SES-2/VMD backplane LEDs so the technician can visually verify the blinking bay before ejecting the carrier.
commands.tip: Never pull a drive without blinking LED
flags: Turn on the blue/amber Locate LED on the backplane slot for the specified block device
Turn off the Locate LED once the drive has been identified
Show SCSI/SAS [Host:Channel:Target:LUN] tuple, SAS transport address, sg device, and size
subs: Reset the drive bay backplane LED back to normal state
Display Device-Mapper Multipath topology, active/passive HBA paths, and LUN WWIDs

linux.html.title: Kernel Modules, GRUB, Serial Console & Burn-in
linux.html.subtitle: modprobe/lsmod/dkms drivers, initramfs, GRUB serial console (ttyS0), kdump & hardware burn-in testing

commands.desc: Inspect loaded kernel modules, check driver version/parameters, and load or unload modules live
commands.details: Verifies which kernel driver module (.ko/.ko.zst) is currently loaded in RAM, its exact version, file path under /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/, and tunable module parameters. Use 'modprobe' to resolve dependencies when loading or unloading drivers.
flags: List loaded kernel modules, memory size, and dependent modules
Show driver path, version, firmware files required, and configurable parameters
subs: Load (-v) or unload (-rv) a kernel module and its unused dependencies
Read currently active runtime parameter values of a loaded kernel module
Check Dynamic Kernel Module Support build/install status across installed Ubuntu kernels

commands.desc: Inspect kernel boot cmdline, configure SOL serial console (ttyS0) in GRUB, and rebuild Ubuntu initramfs
commands.details: Data center servers rely on Serial-over-LAN (IPMI SOL / Redfish Virtual Serial) at 115200 baud when video crashes. Ensure '/etc/default/grub' includes 'console=tty0 console=ttyS0,115200n8' in GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX, then run 'update-grub'.
commands.tip: Essential for IPMI Serial-over-LAN
flags: Exact kernel boot parameters passed by GRUB to the currently running kernel
Send kernel boot & panic output to Serial Port 0 (IPMI SOL) at 115200 baud
subs: Rebuild initial RAM filesystem images for all installed Ubuntu kernels after driver/mdadm changes
Enable interactive login prompt on serial console ttyS0 without rebooting

commands.desc: Inspect application crashes (systemd-coredump) and verify Ubuntu kernel crash dump (kdump) readiness
commands.details: 'coredumpctl' lists user-space processes that terminated with SIGSEGV/SIGABRT and lets you extract backtraces. For full kernel panics on Ubuntu Server (linux-crashdump), 'kdump-config status' verifies that a crashkernel memory reservation is active and ready to capture vmcore dumps to /var/crash.
flags: List captured application core dumps with timestamp, PID, signal, and executable
Check if kexec crash kernel is loaded and ready to capture kernel panics
subs: Show detailed stack trace, registers, and signal metadata for the latest crash
Inspect Ubuntu Apport / kdump crash reports and kernel vmcore directories

commands.desc: Run post-repair hardware burn-in tests on CPU, ECC Memory (stress-ng), and NVMe storage IOPS (fio)
commands.details: After replacing a motherboard, CPU, PSU, or DIMM in the data center, run a controlled thermal and memory verification burn-in before returning the node to production. '--verify' actively checks memory patterns for bit-flips while 'sensors' and 'edac-util' watch for thermal or ECC trips.
commands.tip: Run after CPU/RAM/Motherboard swap
flags: Spawn stressors on all online CPU cores
Test 80% of available RAM with active read/write bit verification (--verify)
Run burn-in test for 10 minutes and print throughput metrics
subs: Benchmark 4K random read IOPS and tail latency (direct I/O bypassing page cache)
Verify IPv6 (-6) 10G/25G/100G/400G NIC throughput across 8 parallel TCP streams for 30 seconds

linux.html.title: Files & Directories
linux.html.subtitle: Navigation, listing, finding, linking & safe manipulation

commands.desc: List all files with human-readable sizes, permissions & hidden dotfiles
commands.details: Displays permission bits, hard link count, owner, group, human-readable byte size, modification timestamp, and filename for every entry including dotfiles starting with '.'.
flags: Long listing format (permissions, owner, size, date)
subs: Sort by modification time in reverse so the newest modified files appear at the bottom
Sort by file size with the largest files at the bottom of the terminal
Include filesystem inode numbers in the first column

commands.desc: Find large or recently modified files across a filesystem without crossing mount boundaries
commands.details: Walks directory trees evaluating predicates on inode metadata. Using '-xdev' prevents descending into mounted network shares, /proc, /sys, or other partitions when hunting down what filled up the root (/) filesystem.
commands.tip: Use -xdev on root '/'
flags: Stay on the same mounted filesystem (do not cross mount points)
Match regular files only (use 'd' for directories, 'l' for symlinks)
Modified less than 7 days ago (-mmin -60 for last 60 minutes)
Batch pass matched paths to a single command invocation (fast)
subs: Find top 20 largest files on the root filesystem with exact byte sizes
Delete rotated compressed logs older than 30 days

commands.desc: Create nested directories, archive-copy preserving attributes, or atomically flip symlinks
commands.details: Combines safe directory creation (-p), archive copying (-a preserves ownership, permissions, ACLs, and symlinks without following them), and atomic symlink replacement (-sfn updates a symlink pointing to a directory in a single rename syscall).
flags: Create parent directories as needed and print each created path
Archive mode (-dR --preserve=all: permissions, timestamps, owners, symlinks)
Create symbolic (-s) link, force overwrite (-f), treat symlink-to-dir as file (-n)
subs: Resolve all symlinks in a path and print the canonical physical path
Display full inode metadata: octal access mode, UID/GID, device ID, links, and Access/Modify/Change/Birth times

commands.desc: Synchronize directories locally or over SSH with delta transfer, progress bar & resume support
commands.details: Uses the rsync delta-transfer algorithm to send only changed blocks over the network while preserving permissions, ownership, timestamps, and symlinks. '-P' combines '--partial' (keep partially transferred files if interrupted) and '--progress'.
commands.tip: Always test --delete with -n first
flags: Archive mode (-rlptgoD: recursive, links, perms, times, group, owner, devices)
Verbose output with human-readable byte counts
Show live transfer progress and keep partial files for resume
Optional: delete extraneous files on destination not present in source
subs: Dry-run (-n) mirror with --delete to preview exactly what would be added or deleted
Throttle transfer bandwidth to 50 MB/s so production NIC traffic is not saturated

linux.html.title: Permissions, Ownership & ACLs
linux.html.subtitle: chmod, chown, POSIX ACLs, setgid shared directories & ext4/xfs immutable attributes

commands.desc: Set standard 755 permissions on directories and 644 on files recursively
commands.details: Directories require the execute (+x) bit so processes can traverse ('cd') into them, whereas regular data files should not be marked executable. Using 'find' or 'chmod +X' separates directory traversal bits from file execution bits.
commands.tip: Fixes SSH & web root permissions
flags: In 'chmod -R u+rwX,go+rX', capital X adds execute only to directories and already-executable files
subs: Smart recursive chmod using capital +X (no find command needed)
Enforce strict SSH directory and key permissions required by sshd StrictModes

commands.desc: Change recursive ownership and set the SGID bit so new files inherit the directory's group
commands.details: Normally, newly created files inherit the primary group of the user who created them. Setting the Set-Group-ID (SGID, octal prefix '2' or 'g+s') bit on a shared directory forces all new files and subdirectories created inside it to inherit the directory's group ownership.
commands.tip: Essential for shared team folders
flags: Recursively set both owner and group across directory tree
rwxrwsr-x: Set-Group-ID on directory so child files inherit group
subs: Set Sticky Bit (octal prefix '1' or '+t') so only a file's owner or root can delete it
commands.rootWhy: gives files to another owner

commands.desc: Grant fine-grained POSIX ACL permissions or lock critical config files with immutable attribute
commands.details: POSIX Access Control Lists (ACLs) grant read/write/execute rights to additional users or groups without changing the base file owner/group. 'chattr +i' sets the ext4/xfs inode immutable bit so even root cannot modify, rename, or delete the file until 'chattr -i' is run.
flags: Modify current file/directory ACL entry for specific user
Set Default ACL on directory so future files automatically inherit the ACL
View base permissions and extended POSIX ACL entries
subs: Strip all extended ACL entries and revert to standard POSIX permissions
Make a file immutable (+i) and inspect extended filesystem attributes (use -i to unlock)

linux.html.title: Text Processing, Log Triage & Streams
linux.html.subtitle: grep, awk, sed, jq, sort, uniq, cut, column & live log pipelines

commands.desc: Search logs or configs recursively with extended regex, line numbers, and surrounding context
commands.details: Scans text files recursively (-r), prints 1-based line numbers (-n), skips binary files (-I), enables extended regex alternation (-E), and shows 2 lines of context before and after each match (-C 2) to understand what triggered an error.
commands.tip: grep -Ev '^\s*(#|$)' strips comments
flags: Print 2 lines of leading (-B) and trailing (-A) context
subs: Strip all comment lines (#) and blank lines to view only active configuration directives
Search source trees excluding version control and dependency directories
Search transparently inside both plain-text and gzip-compressed (.gz) rotated logs

commands.desc: Parse log columns, aggregate metrics with awk, or perform safe in-place edits with sed
commands.details: 'awk' splits each line into whitespace-delimited fields ($1, $2, ... $NF for last field) and runs pattern-action blocks. 'sed -i.bak' performs stream regex substitutions directly on a file while automatically saving a '.bak' copy of the original.
flags: Extract first whitespace-delimited column (use -F':' for custom delimiter)
Count occurrences of adjacent sorted lines
Sort numerically (-n) in reverse descending order (-r)
subs: Sum the 5th column (byte size) across all lines and print total in MiB
Edit config file in-place while creating a .bak backup file automatically
Format any delimiter-separated file or stream into an aligned terminal table

commands.desc: Follow rotating log files live and filter structured JSON output with jq
commands.details: Unlike 'tail -f' (which follows an open file descriptor that stops updating when logrotate renames the file), capital 'tail -F' tracks the filename and automatically reopens the new file after log rotation.
flags: Follow by filename and retry if file is rotated, truncated, or recreated
Output the last 100 lines before following
subs: Parse JSON stream and filter only objects matching a condition
Compare two command outputs on the fly using Bash process substitution

linux.html.title: Processes, Signals, Open Files & Performance
linux.html.subtitle: ps, pgrep/pkill, lsof deleted files, free/vmstat/iostat/pidstat, strace & OOM triage

commands.desc: Find top processes consuming the most Resident Memory (RSS) or CPU, and view process tree
commands.details: Queries /proc/<pid>/stat and status. 'rss' shows physical non-swapped Resident Set Size in KiB; 'stat' shows process state: R (Running), S (Interruptible sleep), D (Uninterruptible I/O sleep — hung NFS/disk), Z (Zombie), T (Stopped).
commands.tip: STAT 'D' = blocked on disk/NFS I/O
flags: Select exact columns to output for every process on the system
Sort descending by physical memory percentage (use -%cpu for CPU)
Uninterruptible sleep (process is blocked inside a kernel I/O syscall)
subs: Run top in non-interactive batch mode sorted by highest CPU utilization
Map any running PID back to its owning systemd service unit and cgroup slice

commands.desc: Find processes holding open file handles to deleted files (fixing 'disk full but du shows space')
commands.details: When a huge log file is deleted ('rm /var/log/huge.log') while a daemon still holds an open file descriptor to it, the kernel does not free the disk blocks until the process closes the FD or restarts. 'lsof +L1' lists every open file with a hard link count less than 1.
commands.tip: Fixes invisible disk exhaustion
flags: List open files with link count < 1 (unlinked / deleted from directory tree)
subs: List all processes holding open files inside the /var/log directory tree
Inspect a process's open file descriptors, binary symlink, and working directory in /proc

commands.desc: Analyze available RAM, buffer/cache breakdown, swap activity, and per-disk I/O latency (await)

cli-tools.html.title: grep — Pattern, Regex & Log Search
cli-tools.html.subtitle: Extended & Perl regex (-E / -P), context lines (-A/-B/-C), comment stripping, zgrep & sysfs multi-file reads

commands.desc: Search logs or directories recursively with Extended Regex, line numbers, binary skip & surrounding context
commands.details: The primary data center log triage command. '-r' walks directories recursively, '-n' prints 1-based line numbers, '-I' skips binary files so they don't corrupt your terminal, '-E' enables Extended Regex alternation '|', and '-C 3' prints 3 lines before and after every match.
commands.tip: Always include -I to skip binaries
flags: Recursive directory search (-R follows all symlinks; -r follows only command-line symlinks)
Prefix each matching output line with its 1-based line number within the file
Process binary files as if they do not match (prevents terminal garbage)
Print 3 lines of leading (-B 3) and trailing (-A 3) context around each match
subs: Show 2 lines before (-B 2) and 5 lines after (-A 5) an OOM-killer trigger
Search only files matching specific filename globs (--include) inside /etc/
Exclude specific directories (--exclude-dir) when searching large trees

commands.desc: Invert match (-v) to strip comments and blank lines from config files or filter out noisy log lines
commands.details: Config files in /etc often have hundreds of '#' or ';' comments and blank lines. 'grep -Ev' inverts the match (-v), printing only active configuration directives.
commands.tip: Instant active-config view
flags: Invert match: select only non-matching lines
Matches lines starting with optional whitespace followed by #, ;, or empty line
subs: Filter out repetitive cron and session noise when inspecting /var/log/syslog
Compare two plain lists and print lines in all_rack_hosts.txt that are missing from known_good_hosts.txt

commands.desc: Extract only the matched token (-o) using Perl-Compatible Regex (-P) lookarounds and \K match reset
commands.details: Adding '-o' (--only-matching) prints ONLY the matched substring on its own line. Combining '-P' (PCRE) with '\K' (keep only what follows '\K') lets you extract values from 'key=value' log lines without sed or awk.
commands.tip: grep -Po 'key=\K\S+' extracts values cleanly
flags: Print only the matched parts of a matching line, each on a separate line
PCRE operator: discard everything matched to the left of \K from the final -o output
subs: Extract only the value after 'user=' using \K without printing 'user=' itself
Extract all unique MAC addresses (XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX) from a log file
Extract all unique PCIe BDF addresses (0000:3b:00.0) mentioned in kernel error logs

commands.desc: List matching filenames (-l / -L), count matches (-c), match whole words (-w), read sysfs (-H '') & zgrep
commands.details: 'grep -H "" /sys/...' is a classic sysadmin trick: since empty pattern '' matches every line and '-H' forces printing the filename prefix, it prints 'filepath:value' for dozens of sysfs pseudo-files in one shot.
commands.tip: grep -H '' /sys/... reads many sysfs files with filenames!
flags: Match whole words only (-w) or whole lines only (-x)
Fixed literal string search (disables regex metacharacters; fastest mode)
Print only filenames WITH matches (-l) or filenames WITHOUT any matches (-L)
Print count of matching lines per file
Always print filename prefix (-H) or suppress filename prefix (-h)
subs: Whole-word search (-w) so '/dev/sda' does not accidentally match '/dev/sda1'
Search across both plain-text and gzip-compressed (.gz) rotated log files transparently

cli-tools.html.title: ps — Process, Thread & State Inspection
cli-tools.html.subtitle: Custom -eo columns, STAT state triage, hung D-state kernel wchan, CPU core affinity (psr) & thread views

commands.desc: Display custom process table sorted by Resident Memory (RSS) or CPU% with exact start time and PPID
commands.details: 'ps -eo <columns>' lets you specify the exact kernel process fields you need without truncating usernames and sort descending (-) or ascending (+) by any metric ('--sort=-%mem', '--sort=-%cpu', '--sort=-rss', '--sort=etimes').
commands.tip: nlwp shows thread count per process
flags: Select every process running on the system
User-defined columns (pid, ppid, nlwp=thread count, rss=resident KiB, etimes=elapsed secs)
Sort descending (-) or ascending (+) by any specified column key
Render ASCII art parent-child process tree
subs: List top 15 CPU-consuming processes along with elapsed runtime in seconds (etimes)
Display full ASCII process hierarchy tree showing parent-child spawning relationships

commands.desc: Diagnose hung Uninterruptible I/O ('D' state) processes, kernel wait channels (wchan) & Zombie ('Z') parents
commands.details: When an NFS mount hangs or a RAID/NVMe controller stalls, processes enter 'D' state (Uninterruptible sleep inside a kernel syscall) and ignore SIGKILL (-9). Inspecting 'wchan' (Kernel Wait Channel) and '/proc/<PID>/stack' reveals the exact kernel function where the process is blocked.
commands.tip: Kill Parent (PPID) to clear Zombies; fix I/O to clear D-state
flags: Process state: D = Uninterruptible I/O sleep, Z = Zombie (defunct), R = Running, S = Sleeping
Name of the kernel function in which the process is sleeping (widened to 28 chars)
subs: Print the live kernel call stack of the oldest process currently stuck in 'D' state
ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,comm | awk '$3 ~ /^Z/ {print "Zombie PID:", $1, "-> Parent PPID:", $2, $4}'
Identify Zombie processes and print the Parent PID (PPID) that failed to reap them

commands.desc: Inspect individual threads (LWP/TID), see which physical CPU core (psr) each thread is running on & check cgroups
commands.details: 'ps -eL' expands every process into its individual Light Weight Processes (threads / LWP) and 'psr' shows the exact logical CPU core ID currently executing that thread.
commands.tip: psr column reveals CPU pinning & core hotspots
flags: Show individual threads with LWP / SPID (Thread ID) and NLWP columns
Processor / logical CPU core ID currently executing the thread
Display systemd slice / container cgroup path owning the process
subs: List all threads belonging to a single PID along with their assigned CPU core (psr)
Map running PIDs back to their owning systemd .service or container cgroup slice
Safely match or signal processes by full command line using pgrep/pkill

Sort by mtime newest first (-t), file size largest first (-S), or natural version (-v)

Show last access/read timestamp (atime) or metadata change timestamp (--time=ctime)
Inspect permissions and ownership of directory entries themselves (-d)

cli-tools.html.title: stat — Inode & Filesystem Metadata

commands.desc: Inspect complete file inode metadata (timestamps, octal mode, UID/GID, links) or filesystem-level block/inode counters

cli-tools.html.title: namei — Path & Symlink Permission Chain Resolver
cli-tools.html.subtitle: Walking every parent directory and symlink from '/' down to a target path to spot broken permissions or loops

commands.desc: Trace every directory component and symlink from root '/' down to a file with permissions and ownership at each hop
commands.details: When a service fails with 'Permission denied' even though the target file itself is 644/755, one of its parent directories (/var, /var/www, or a symlink target) is usually missing the execute (+x) traversal bit. 'namei -l' prints permissions for every step in the path chain.
commands.tip: Instantly spots missing '+x' on parent directories
flags: Long listing format: display permissions, owner, and group for each path component
Show the mode bits of each file type in the path
Show owner and group name of each component
Show mount point directories with a 'D' instead of 'd'

cli-tools.html.title: file — Binary, Filesystem & Magic Header Identifier
cli-tools.html.subtitle: Inspecting ELF binaries, core dumps, raw disk partition headers (-s), and compressed archives via magic bytes

commands.desc: Identify file types, ELF architecture, compression format, or raw block partition filesystems via magic bytes
commands.details: Instead of trusting file extensions, 'file' reads magic byte signatures inside the file header. Try to look inside compressed files (.gz, .xz, .zst) to identify the inner payload

Peek inside a compressed file to see the uncompressed archive format and original timestamp

cli-tools.html.title: awk — Column Processing, Math & Associative Arrays
cli-tools.html.subtitle: Field splitting (-F), built-in variables (NR/NF/FNR), conditional filtering, math summaries & array grouping

commands.desc: Extract, reorder, and format specific columns using whitespace or custom regex field delimiters (-F)
commands.details: By default, awk splits each line on runs of whitespace and assigns columns to $1, $2, ... $NF (where $NF is the last column and $0 is the whole line). Use '-F' to split on ':', ',', or a regex character class like '-F"[/: ]+"'.
commands.tip: NR>1 skips the header row of CLI tables
flags: Set Input Field Separator (FS) to ':' (or regex like -F'[,;:\t]+')
Positional column variables ($NF = last column, $(NF-1) = second-to-last column)

Formatted C-style output (%-15s = left-aligned 15-char string, %.2f = 2-decimal float)

Print only UP network interfaces and their primary IPv4 CIDR address

commands.cmd: ps -eo rss,comm | awk 'NR>1 {sum+=$1; count++; if($1>max){max=$1; maxp=$2}} END {printf "Procs:%d  Total:%.1f MiB  Avg:%.1f MiB  Max:%s (%.1f MiB)\n", count, sum/1024, (sum/count)/1024, maxp, max/1024}'
commands.desc: Calculate sum, average, min, and max across numeric columns in logs or command outputs
commands.details: Code inside the main '{...}' block runs once for every matching input line, and the 'END {...}' block runs after all input lines have been processed to print totals, averages, and maximums.
flags: Executed once before any input lines are read
Executed once after EOF is reached across all inputs
subs: ls -l /var/log/*.log | awk '{sum += $5} END {printf "Total uncompressed logs: %.2f MiB\n", sum/1048576}'
Sum byte sizes (column 5 of ls -l) and print total in MiB
awk '{sum+=$NF; n++} END {if (n>0) print "Average:", sum/n}' timing.log

copy: ps -eo rss,comm | awk 'NR>1 {sum+=$1; count++; if($1>max){max=$1; maxp=$2}} END {printf "Procs:%d  Total:%.1f MiB  Avg:%.1f MiB  Max:%s (%.1f MiB)\n", count, sum/1024, (sum/count)/1024, maxp, max/1024}'

Deduplicate repeated lines in a file without sorting (preserves chronological order)

copy: ss -tan | awk 'NR>1 {state[$1]++} END {for (s in state) printf "%-15s %d\n", s, state[s]}' | sort -k2 -nr

commands.details: 'sed -n "/START/,/END/p"' streams only the lines between the first occurrence of START and the END marker. For line numbers, add 'q' after the end line ('sed -n "1000,1050p;1051q"') so sed stops reading the rest of a huge file immediately.

cli-tools.html.title: sudo & root — Why Root Is Dangerous and How to Use sudo
cli-tools.html.subtitle: What root is, what can go wrong as root, why sudo is safer than a root login, and the sudo options you use on the job

commands.desc: Why not just work as root? The dangers, and what sudo does instead
commands.details: 1) No safety net: rm -rf on the wrong path, dd, mkfs or wipefs on the wrong disk, chmod -R or chown -R on / all just happen. 2) Everything inherits root: every program, script, plugin and editor shell escape started from a root shell runs as root, so a bad install script or a compromised package owns the machine. 3) No accountability: with a shared root password the logs only say root. 4) Root shells linger: a forgotten root shell in tmux or on a jumpbox is an open door. sudo answers each one: root for one command at a time, your own password, your user name and command in the log, cached for 5 minutes by default, and sudoers can allow only the commands you need (least privilege).
commands.tip: Root is a tool for one step, not a place to work
flags: Root only for the command that needs it, then you are back to your normal user
No shared root password to leak or rotate when someone leaves
Who ran what, where and when: needed for audits and incident timelines
Your password is cached for 5 minutes by default (sudoers timestamp_timeout); sudo -k ends it now
sudoers can allow one command (for example ipmitool) instead of everything
Lists exactly what you are allowed to run here
subs: Forget your cached password now (do it before you walk away)
Refresh the cache without running anything (before a long series of steps)

commands.desc: Who am I running as? Check before you type anything destructive
commands.details: root is the account with user ID 0. For root the kernel skips most permission checks: any file can be read, changed or deleted, any disk can be overwritten, any process can be killed. That is exactly why it is dangerous: the system stops protecting you from your own typo. A prompt ending in # usually means you are root; $ means a normal user.
commands.tip: Read the prompt: # means every command is unchecked
flags: You are root right now: nothing checks your permissions
You may use sudo (Ubuntu and Debian use the sudo group; RHEL and Rocky use wheel)
Usually a root shell. Exit it as soon as the job is done
The root password is locked by default: you are meant to use sudo, not log in as root
subs: What sudo lets you run on this host (asks for your password)

commands.desc: Run one command as root, or as another user
commands.details: sudo checks the sudoers policy, asks for YOUR password (not root's), runs the command as root and logs it. On this site, and in the agent's answers, commands that need root are marked # needs root instead of carrying a sudo prefix: you decide how to elevate.
commands.tip: Prefix the one command, never your whole session
flags: Run as that user instead of root, for example a service account: sudo -u postgres psql
Never prompt: fail with an error if a password is needed (use in scripts so they never hang)
End the cached password now / refresh it
End of sudo's own options: everything after it belongs to the command
Re-runs your previous command as root. Read it again first: !! is whatever ran last
subs: Run a command as a service account
sudo -n true && echo 'sudo works without a prompt'
Check that a script can use sudo before it runs
commands.rootWhy: root where kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1 (Ubuntu 20.10+, Arch); check: sysctl kernel.dmesg_restrict

commands.desc: A root shell when you really need one: sudo -i, sudo -s and su
commands.details: Sometimes a root shell is the practical choice (a long recovery in single-user style). Know the trade-off: sudo logs only the command it runs, so once you are in a root shell the commands you type there are not logged one by one (the sudo man page warns about exactly this). Get in, do the job, type exit.
commands.tip: If you open a root shell, close it in the same breath
flags: Login shell as root: root's environment and home directory, reads root's profile
Shell as root that keeps your own environment (your $HOME, PATH may be reset by policy)
Switch to root with ROOT's password: on Ubuntu root's password is locked, so this usually fails
Same as a root shell, and it skips the per-command log: avoid
Leave the root shell the moment you are done

commands.desc: The redirect gotcha: sudo echo > /etc/file fails; use tee (changes state)
commands.details: In sudo echo x > /etc/file, your own shell opens /etc/file for the > BEFORE sudo runs, so it fails with Permission denied. Piping into sudo tee makes tee (running as root) open the file. Add > /dev/null to hide tee's echo, and -a to append instead of replace.
commands.tip: The shell does the redirect, not sudo
flags: tee opens the file as root, so the write works
Append instead of replacing the file
Stop tee from also printing the text to your screen
The other fix: the whole line, redirect included, runs as root
subs: Append a line to a root-owned file (changes state)
commands.rootWhy: writes into /etc, /sys, /proc or /boot

commands.desc: Edit a root-owned file safely with sudoedit (sudo -e)
commands.details: sudoedit copies the file to a temporary file owned by you, runs YOUR editor as you, and writes the result back as root only when you save. Your editor, its plugins and its shell escapes never run as root, unlike sudo nano or sudo vim. Back up first, validate after (sshd -t, visudo -c, findmnt --verify).
commands.tip: Back up, sudoedit, then validate
flags: Pick the editor it uses, for example SUDO_EDITOR=nano
Inside sudo vim, :!bash gives a root shell that is not logged

commands.desc: Who may run what: sudoers drop-in files, edited only with visudo (changes state)
commands.details: Never edit /etc/sudoers or its drop-ins with a plain editor: one syntax error can leave nobody able to use sudo. visudo locks the file and checks the syntax before saving. Grant the smallest set of commands that does the job. Be careful with NOPASSWD (no password at all) and with commands that can start a shell (editors, less, find -exec, tar --to-command): each one is a way to a full root shell.
commands.tip: Keep a second root session open while you change sudoers
flags: Edit a drop-in in /etc/sudoers.d/ with locking and a syntax check
Check every sudoers file without editing
Example rule: members of a group may run only ipmitool as root
Skips the password: convenient for automation, risky on a shared account
On Ubuntu's newer sudo-rs, visudo is reported to check only /etc/sudoers itself, not the drop-ins: verify on your release
subs: Syntax check of every sudoers file
commands.rootWhy: changes accounts or sudo rules

commands.desc: Who ran what as root? Read the sudo log
commands.details: Every sudo command is logged with the user, the terminal, the working directory and the full command. That is what makes sudo better than a shared root login during an incident: the timeline shows who changed what. Ubuntu and Debian also write it to /var/log/auth.log; RHEL and Rocky to /var/log/secure.
commands.tip: Commands typed inside a root shell do not show up here
commands.rootWhy: the system journal needs root or the systemd-journal / adm group

commands.desc: Which sudo is this? Ubuntu 25.10 and 26.04 default to sudo-rs
commands.details: Ubuntu now ships sudo-rs, a Rust rewrite of sudo, as the default, and keeps the original as sudo.ws. Day-to-day use is the same. Reported differences: sudo-rs shows asterisks while you type the password, visudo checks less, and some sudoers features (LDAP sudoers, mail on failure) are not supported. Upstream sudo is at 1.9.17p2.
commands.tip: If a sudoers rule behaves differently on Ubuntu 26.04, check which sudo is active
flags: The original sudo, still installed as a fallback

sudo.html.subtitle: Why not just work as root? The dangers, and what sudo does instead

commands.desc: Why not just work as root? The dangers, and what sudo does instead
commands.details: 1) No safety net: rm -rf on the wrong path, dd, mkfs or wipefs on the wrong disk, chmod -R or chown -R on / all just happen. 2) Everything inherits root: every program, script, plugin and editor shell escape started from a root shell runs as root, so a bad install script or a compromised package owns the machine. 3) No accountability: with a shared root password the logs only say root. 4) Root shells linger: a forgotten root shell in tmux or on a jumpbox is an open door. sudo answers each one: root for one command at a time, your own password, your user name and command in the log, cached for 5 minutes by default, and sudoers can allow only the commands you need (least privilege).
commands.tip: Root is a tool for one step, not a place to work
flags: Root only for the command that needs it, then you are back to your normal user
No shared root password to leak or rotate when someone leaves
Who ran what, where and when: needed for audits and incident timelines
Your password is cached for 5 minutes by default (sudoers timestamp_timeout); sudo -k ends it now
sudoers can allow one command (for example ipmitool) instead of everything
Lists exactly what you are allowed to run here

That is exactly why it is dangerous: the system stops protecting you from your own typo. A prompt ending in # usually means you are root; $ means a normal user.

commands.cmd:
import json
from pathlib import Path

file_path = Path("/etc/datacenter/config.json")

try:
    # Safe context manager: auto-closes file even on error
    with open(file_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        data = json.load(f)
except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"Config file missing: {file_path}")
    data = {}
except json.JSONDecodeError as err:
    print(f"Malformed JSON on line {err.lineno}: {err.msg}")
    raise SystemExit(1)
finally:
    print("Execution finished")

  local count = 0

  local total = 0

commands.cmd:
-- Query nodes with high GPU temperature and join rack info
SELECT 
  n.hostname,
  n.ip_address,
  r.name AS rack_name,
  COUNT(g.id) AS gpu_count,
  AVG(g.temp_c) AS avg_temp
FROM nodes n
INNER JOIN racks r ON n.rack_id = r.id
LEFT JOIN gpus g ON n.id = g.node_id
WHERE n.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY n.id
HAVING avg_temp > 75.0
ORDER BY avg_temp DESC
LIMIT 20;

If bandwidth is capped around ~250 Gb/s, check 'lspci -vvv' to see if the slot downgraded to PCIe Gen4!

commands.details: TDR (Time-Domain Reflectometry) transmits electrical pulses into twisted pairs to measure impedance reflections, detecting open pairs, shorts, and distance to faults within 1 meter accuracy. Installation of Southbridge Runtime Services (62) and CPU DXE initialization started (63)

commands.desc: PCIe Bus Hangs, Bifurcation & Option ROM Freeze Triage
commands.details: Codes 0x91–0x96 occur during DXE driver dispatch and bus enumeration. A hang at 0x94 (PCI Bus Enumeration) indicates an unseated riser, bad PCIe Gen5 retimer, or shorted power pins on a multi-GPU add-in card. 0xd6 indicates No Console Output Found (missing or disabled GPU display output).
commands.tip: Verify PCIe bifurcation settings in BIOS: setting an x16 slot to x4x4x4x4 for quad M.2 cards avoids post code 0x94 hangs.
flags: PCIe bus scan failure: unseated riser, bad cable, or dead add-in card
PCI resource allocation failure: enable "Above 4G Decoding" and Large BARs
No VGA display device detected: verify primary display selection in BMC

mb-storage-bds-post.html.subtitle: Decode SATA, SAS, M.2 NVMe, and USB bus initialization codes (`0x99`–`0xA7`, `0xB4`)

commands.cmd: POST 0x99 (Super IO)  ->  0x9C (USB Detect)  ->  0xA0 (IDE/AHCI Init)  ->  0xA2 (Drive Detect)  ->  0xB4 (USB Hotplug)
commands.desc: Decode SATA, SAS, M.2 NVMe, and USB bus initialization codes (`0x99`–`0xA7`, `0xB4`)
commands.tip: Stuck on 0xA2 = unplug SATA/M.2 drives one by one to find the bad drive!
flags: Super I/O initialization (99) and USB controller initialization started (9A)
USB Detect (9C — probing USB ports, KVM dongles, and BMC Virtual Media) and USB Enable (9D)
IDE / SATA AHCI controller initialization started (A0) and reset (A1)
IDE / SATA / M.2 Drive Detect (A2) and Enable (A3): Hang at 0xA2 = dead SATA DOM, failing M.2 SSD, or bad backplane SATA cable!
SCSI / SAS / NVMe backplane bus initialization (A4), reset (A5), and detect (A6)
USB Hot-Plug: Frequent pause point when a faulty USB flash drive or corrupted BMC Virtual Media ISO is mounted
copy: POST 0x99 (Super IO)  ->  0x9C (USB Detect)  ->  0xA0 (IDE/AHCI Init)  ->  0xA2 (Drive Detect)  ->  0xB4 (USB Hotplug)

mb-storage-bds-post.html.title: Storage & Boot BDS: Decode UEFI Setup entry, PXE/NVMe boot selection, and OS handoff codes
mb-storage-bds-post.html.subtitle: Decode UEFI Setup entry, PXE/NVMe boot selection, and OS handoff codes (`0xA9`–`0xAE`, `0xAA`, `0x00`)

commands.cmd: POST 0xA9 (Start Setup)  ->  0xAB (Setup Input Wait)  ->  0xAD (Ready To Boot)  ->  0xAA / 0x00 (OS Running)
commands.desc: Decode UEFI Setup entry, PXE/NVMe boot selection, and OS handoff codes (`0xA9`–`0xAE`, `0xAA`, `0x00`)
commands.tip: 0xAB means the board is waiting at the BIOS prompt (connect BMC KVM/SOL)!
flags: Start of Setup (A9) and Setup Input Wait (AB): The server is NOT hung — it is sitting inside BIOS Setup or waiting for F1 on VGA/SOL!
Reserved for ASL / Entering UEFI Shell or boot menu selection
Ready To Boot Event: UEFI POST is 100% finished and handing control to GRUB / Linux EFI stub / PXE NBP
Legacy Boot Event: Handing control to a legacy MBR bootloader
System has transitioned into ACPI APIC mode — OS is booted and running normally (ASUS Q-Code often rests on AA or A0 in Ubuntu)
If stuck on 0x00 or 0xFF the instant power is pressed: CPU not executing reset vector (check 8-pin EPS12V cables, CPU VRMs, or BIOS flash)
copy: POST 0xA9 (Start Setup)  ->  0xAB (Setup Input Wait)  ->  0xAD (Ready To Boot)  ->  0xAA / 0x00 (OS Running)

commands.desc: Storage Detection, Boot Device Selection (BDS) & OS Handoff
commands.details: Codes starting with 0xA indicate Boot Device Selection (BDS). A hang at 0xA2 (IDE/SATA Detect) typically points to a failing NVMe SSD, corrupt M.2 controller, or degraded backplane cable. 0xAA indicates successfully passing control to the ACPI OS (normal operating state).
commands.tip: 0xAD (Ready To Boot) means the system is waiting for boot media; check efibootmgr order or PXE timeout.
flags: SATA/NVMe drive detection hang: bad drive controller or broken backplane link
UEFI handoff pending: check USB installer, NVMe bootloader, or PXE target

mb-epyc-agesa.html.subtitle: Understand the 2-Stage POST sequence on GIGABYTE & ASUS AMD EPYC (Rome/Milan/Genoa/Turin) boards

commands.cmd: Stage 1: AMD PSP & AGESA BootLoader (0xE0..0xFF / 0xD0..0xDF)   -->   Stage 2: AMI Aptio V UEFI (0x10..0xAD)
commands.desc: Understand the 2-Stage POST sequence on GIGABYTE & ASUS AMD EPYC (Rome/Milan/Genoa/Turin) boards
commands.tip: EPYC SP3/SP5 sockets are extremely torque-sensitive: uneven Torx T20 screws cause 0xEA/0x55!
flags: On AMD EPYC (SP3/SP5), the integrated Platform Security Processor (PSP) and AGESA BootLoader (ABL) initialize Infinity Fabric and DDR4/DDR5 BEFORE x86 cores start AMI UEFI!
ABL0/ABL1: Early processor & memory parameter initialization and SPD readout across all 8 or 12 memory channels
ABL2/ABL3: PMU (PHY Microcontroller Unit) DDR4/DDR5 training across populated DIMM channels
ABL Memory Training Error: PMU failed to train a DDR4/DDR5 channel (reseat DIMMs, check CPU socket torque of 12.0–13.5 in-lbs on Torx T20)
ABL Stage complete — releasing x86 Zen cores from reset to begin AMI Aptio V SEC/PEI (0x10+)
copy: Stage 1: AMD PSP & AGESA BootLoader (0xE0..0xFF / 0xD0..0xDF)   -->   Stage 2: AMI Aptio V UEFI (0x10..0xAD)

commands.desc: Diagnose Dual-Socket (2P) AMD EPYC Infinity Fabric (xGMI) & Intel Xeon UPI link training hangs
commands.tip: You can flash BIOS via ASUS ASMB11 or GIGABYTE GSM BMC even without a supported CPU installed!

On GIGABYTE MZ72/MZ73 & ASUS KRPA-U16/K14PA: if 2P board halts on 0xE4 or 0xB7, check BMC SEL to see if error is on P0 (Socket 0) or P1 (Socket 1)

commands.details: AMD EPYC motherboards exhibit a unique 2-stage POST cycle. The Platform Security Processor (PSP) boots first, displaying E0–FF codes on port 0x80 while loading microcode and initializing CPU chiplets. The board then resets and executes standard AMI Aptio PEI/DXE codes.

argocd.html.title: Argo CD: Pro Tip
argocd.html.subtitle: Automated sync with prune and self-heal

commands.cmd:
spec:
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
commands.desc: Automated sync with prune and self-heal
commands.details: automated: {} alone syncs on Git changes but never deletes; prune: true deletes resources removed from Git; selfHeal: true reverts manual changes in the cluster. The same from the CLI: argocd app set <app> --sync-policy automated --auto-prune --self-heal.
commands.tip: With selfHeal on, a hotfix made with kubectl is undone: change Git instead
copy:
spec:
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
